speechtext: Shame 1

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTED-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO.
speechtext:
And the intrigues were still being carried on, Sir, the case goes from worse to worse. According to a letter dated August 25, 1920, addressed to
5122	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Sylvestre
the Deputy Minister by the crown attorneys, the following is to be found:
Sir,-Section 1028 of the Crimiraail Code provides that whenever the offender shall be liable to different degrees or kinds of ,punishment, .the punishment to be inflicted shall subject to the limitations contained in the enactment, be in the discretion of the court or tribunal before which the conviction took place.
It is true.
It would appear this applies to section 1080 of the Inland Revenue Act, which imposes both fine and imprisonment. In fact this was decided in the case of Rex vs. Robiidoux, 2, C.C.C. page 19, and also ex,parte Kent, 7, C.C.C. page 447. It was ruled in these cases that unless there is express provision to the contrary, an enactment which authorizes both fine and imprisonment for the summary conviction the offence is to be construed as giving discretion to the magistrate to impose fine or imprisonment, or both.
That is the crown attorney wrote a letter which is absolutely in keeping with the provisions contained in the Statutes. When a penalty includes a fine and imprisonment, it is according to law, and it was decided in the cases cited that the judge may impose one or the other or both at the same time. The judge, yes, but not the crown. The government has no right to direct the judge, as it was done in this oase, to act in such and such a way, to influence his decision, to dictate to him his duty. Mr. Speaker, never have we witnessed such a disgusting procedure; here we find a minister, who for purely political aims, being fully aware of the situation and having to deal with a dangerous criminal, instructs the department to begin overtures in order to give this dangerous criminal his freedom. The letter continues:
If you refer /to these decisions you will note that they were given with regard to prosecution taken under section 180 Oif the Inland Revenue Act, which is section 150 of the old act, so that there ds not, in my mind, the slightest doulbt that section 1028 of the Criminal Code applies to all prosecutions taken under above quoted section of the Inland Revenue Aot.
This a.parently does not satisify Mr. Justice Choquette of Quebec City, before whom the department has taken a certain number of prosecutions, under section 180 of the Inland Revenue Aot. Mr. Justice Choquette claims that as this section provides for both fine and imprisonment, he has no other alternative than to send him to jail, if the department may not insist on itlie imprisonment portion of the sentence. He has therefore requested the department, before rendering sentence, in each case, to obtain your opinion as to whether or not he may dispense with the imprtiisoaiiment, and I shall be glad to have you advise me in this regard at your earliest convenience.
As the sentence against the parties concerned has been suspended pending expression of your opinion, I would request you to give the matter your immediate attention.
Now, it is included in the evidence that the department at that time took serious steps and proceedings in order to try to influence the decision of Judge Choquette who

wanted to sentence the man to both a fine /and imprisonment, as it was his right, and they endeav-oured.to find some way out, some means in order to protect a dangerous Criminal by simply imposing a fine.
, And this, Sir, did not occur under a Liberal government, it did not occur under the reign pf those who, according to the Tories, have po knowledge even of what may mean the word virtue, but it did take place under a Tory administration, under the reign of our good Conservatives, under those who are shocked at a trifling, under the government of those gentlemen who are not aware that they are living in glass houses and that it is very dangerous for them to throw stones into their neighbour's garden; all this happened under the over virtuous administration which held power from 1911 to 1921!
These gentlemen were in too great a hurry to cross over to your right, Sir, where they are at present, I' am confident that they will still make a quicker crossing to this side which they have just left.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
The House resumed, from June 22, consideration in committee of Bill No. 95, to incorporate the Red Lake and Northwestern Railway Company-Mr. Heenan-Mr. Duff in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.
iMr. CHURCH:	I do not wish the House
to think I am taking an unfair attitude in regard to this bill, but there is a great public principle involved; the whole railway question of Canada is wrapped up in the principle involved in this particular bill. The province of Ontario is vitally interested in it; the territory to be covered is a part of the newer section of Ontario, and I believe it to be National railway territory. No matter on what side of the House I sit, I support my principles first, last and all the time, and I believe a great question of public rights is before the House now. The people of Canada have spent two billion dollars on railways and to-day the policy of Sir Henry Thornton is pro-American. He has millions of dollars in Vermont and millions of dollars in Michigan, but he has no money to build branch lines into the richest territory in Canada. The wealth of this country is unknown and unexplored; it contains about 4,000 prospectors, who require this service.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that the province of Ontario, which according to a return which I received from the Deputy Minister of Railways only yesterday, pays $780,000 a year to the Dominion government out of a total revenue of $946,000, should receive more consideration. The young ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) and the Progressives succeeded in having $28,000,000 spent on branch lines in the west for the benefit of agriculture. I am a supporter of New Ontario ; I supported it in the old days when we wanted iSir Adam Beck to electrify the Temis-kaming and Northern Ontario railway in order to preserve the great mineral wealth of that country for the people of Ontario. Now that wealth is controlled by American capital, together with the water-powers existing there. Once you give away the water-power you automatically give away the dominant factol in the industrial life of the country, and I contend that if the Canadian National Railways can afford to spend $28,000,000 on branch
lines in the west they can afford to build a branch line here and preserve this territory.
I believe I am representing a great public policy and a great public principle in forcing a showdown with the administration of the National railways, so that New Ontario will be given -what it deserves. I do not want the young member for North Timiskaming (Mr. O'Neill) to think I am opposing this bill because of any personal reason, but I want to see justice done to that territory not only by this House, but by t'he government of the province of Ontario as well. The Toronto Globe has been running a series of articles dealing with the Red lake district, its wealth and its transportation needs. I opposed this bill in the Railway committee on public grounds, because I believe Ontario to-day is only a way-station for the rest of Canada. Speaking of a ginger group, I believe that is the thing we in Ontario need; no province is suffering more to-day from a lack of transportation than is Ontario. The old Grand Trunk railway in Ontario was taken over by the government, and the money which should have been invested there was put into the National Transcontinental railway. What was the result. From that day to this the older sections of Ontario, as well as new Ontario, have been suffering untold ills from the lack of transportation; farmers have been unable to get their crops to market, there has been rural depopulation and lack of production.
In referring to the principle involved in this bill, I wish to quote from the report prepared in part by the present Acting Minister of Railways, the Drayton-Acworth report, which has a direct bearing on this particular charter. This report was made to parliament in 1917, after an exhaustive survey of the waste and duplication of railways in this country, railways that had been built without any possible hope of making dividends, let alone interest and sinking charges. This report says:
We recommend that the jurisdiction of the railway commission should be enlarged. Charters for new railways are granted by the Dominion parliament in great numbers. In the years from 1900 to 1908, 116 charters were granted for 37,862 miles of line. Only 453 miles were actually built. In the two following yeans there were granted, according (to a statement made in the Senate by the Hon. Mr. Davis, on April 6, 1910, respectively, 68 charters for about 68,000 miles and 75 charters for about 75,000 miles.
The commission further recommends:
We think that no charter should be granted, til! the *proposals made have been investigated by the commission, and the commission have reported whether or not, in their opinion, the construction of the proposed line would be fo-r the public advantage. The opinion of the commission will not necessarily bind the action of parliament.

speechtext:
It is well known that Mr. Backus went to the Ontario legislature in the days of the Farmer-Labour government, and that that government gave to Mr. Backus a whole kingdom up in New Ontario. Mr. Backus wrote a letter to the Railway committee offering to build this railway himself. I want to criticize the policy of Sir Henry Thornton and of the National Railways for giving up this territory. The other night we passed a vote of $3,000,000 for the Hudson Bay railway, and here it is proposed to build a line that will take away business from that railway. The province of Ontario has been sidetracked so far as branch lines are concerned.
So far as the principle of this bill is concerned, this is not a project for the general advantage of Canada. It cannot be considered such by the wildest stretch of imagination. The railway is to be built wholly within Ontario, and the promoters should have gone to the Toronto legislature for their charter. It was admitted that to come within the jurisdiction of this parliament the road technically had to cross the border into Manitoba. The Minister of Railways was asked in the railway committee what the policy of the government was regarding this particular railway, and he could not tell the committee. The National Railways have millions of dollars to spend on golf links and hotels and improving the system in the United States, in Michigan and Vermont, but when it comes to developing the mining industry of this country, where are they? We allow private interests, largely American, to get these franchises, and I say that it is the duty of

this parliament to stop issuing these paper charters. We have a new Acting Minister of Railways, and his report was on the right lines when he recommended that we should go slow in granting such charters as this. This bill, Mr. Chairman, is 95 per cent a mining and a power bill, instead of a transportation proposition. I protest against the province of Ontario, which contributes 46 per cent of	the	taxation collected	by	thetreasury of this country, being sidetracked in the matter of branch lines. In Manitoba and Saskatchewan the National Railways are building branch	lines that will never	paydividends, let alone interest charges, and as one of the representatives of Ontario I protest against	the	shortsighted policy	of	theNational Railways in failing to give Ontario the branch lines it needs, not only in the older parts of the province, but in the newer portions, in	the	Red lake district,	for	instance, and other portions of the province where branch lines are required to develop the mining industry in this province.
The richest mining country in the world today lies in the northwest section of the province of Ontario, including the Red lake district; as far as the Manitoba boundary, and also in the Cobalt and other districts where mines are being worked. This being the case I am sorry at the shortsightedness of the government of Ontario in writing to the Railway committee of the House of Commons and saying they had no interest in this bill. If there is one district in which the government of Ontario should be interested, it is New Ontario with its untold wealth. There are approximately 4,000 prospectors in the Red lake district at the present time and they can get a good road in there for a very small amount of money. But every member from Ontario who is loyal to his province should be in favour of the National railways building into that territory. If this bill passes, then good-bye to any possibility that Sir Henry Thornton and the National railways will do anything to develop this part of northern Ontario. Sir Henry Thornton has already spent millions of dollars on building golf courses and installing radios, on giving terminals to Detroit, and providing facilities in the state of Vermont, but when it comes to developing New Ontario that gentleman has no money at all available. I suppose if a branch line to the North Pole were needed he would not find it difficult to obtain the necessary financial aid. I am sorry that the mining industry of the province of Ontario has not received the support which it should have received. One of the greatest mistakes made by the late Sir James Whitney-and he
did not make many mistakes-was in failing to electrify the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway, and undertaking to provide cheap light and power for the miners and. prospectors in northern Ontario. Had he done that, New Ontario would have had a population of half a million people instead of a population of 80,000, and the gold and silver production of the province would be ten or fifteen times what it is at present. A further result would have been that the population of Ontario would have grown to such a figure that it would have been entitled to a representation of ten more members in this House, and then that province would have got justice from this parliament. It is really most discouraging and most humiliating that the tax payers of Ontario, who pay 46 per cent of the taxation of Canada, cannot get one necessary branch line built into the northern districts of the province where untold wealth is waiting to be mined.

maintopic: BED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Coming from the north country and being very closely allied with its interests I wish to speak on this question for a few minutes. We who went to northern Ontario before the advent of railroads are thoroughly familiar with its problems. We had hoped in past years that the provincial and the Dominion governments would be the chief agents in developing the great industries of northern Ontario. I was a member of a delegation which interviewed Sir Adam Beck and asked him to get the Hydro Electric Commission to develop power in New Ontario. We were flatly turned down on that occasion. We were told that the Hydro Electric would not undertake the development of power in the north country; it would cost them more than it would cost private interests. At that time we were paying $250 per horsepower in the mines but to-day as a result of development by private interests it costs only from $50 to $60 per horse-power. There would not have been a wheel turned in the north country to-day if it had not been for the ingenuity and the energy of private.interests. I believe that if it were possible the Ontario government and the Dominion authorities should come in and carry on development work; but if they will not do so why should private interests be debarred from doing the necessary development? I say here to-night that there would not have been many mines discovered in northern Ontario if we had relied only on the provincial or federal government. Every mine discovered there has been discovered by a prospector, the pioneer of the north country.

Red Lake Railway Company

maintopic: BED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: How were the nickel mines at Sudbury and the silver mines at Cobalt discovered except through public ownership and the construction of a railroad by the government of the late Sir James Whitney? That country was not developed by prospectors, it was developed as a result of the policy of Sir James Whitney in causing a railway to be built through the mining district.

maintopic: BED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
No
mine was discovered by any. government. Both the Larose and the McKinley-Darragh mines were discovered by prospectors, not by the Whitney government. The provincial government, it is true, sent a prospecting party to co-operate with the prospectors. They also started a property known as the Provincial Mine, but it was not followed up and it turned out to be a dud. Since then the provincial government have entirely abandoned the policy of prospecting the north country; they have left it entirely to the prospectors, who are deserving of credit for the energy and heroism which they have displayed. I want to say another thing for those prospectors. In that country we are greatly indebted to prospectors who go into remote districts and make discoveries, although they have no money and scarcely anything but a grubstake. They have to take in their train a canoe in the summer or a dog-team in the winter. It costs twice the price of the ordinary express on the National Railways. That is what the National Railways do to assist prospecting. It is almost impossible for some of the poor prospectors to take their equipment from Cobalt to a point west of Red lake. Some interest must be shown in the prospectors.
We have attached great importance in past years to the work of the pioneers in agriculture. The agricultural area in our country depends entirely upon the mining area. You cannot send your agricultural products out of our country; the agriculturists have to depend upon the mining people for a market, and mining and agriculture in our part of the country go hand in hand. Since I came to that country more than a hundred thousand people have been brought in. If the government do not intend to do something in this connection they should give private ownership an opportunity. I am not speaking particularly in favour of this railroad or against it, but I am in favour of allowing private enterprise an opportunity of building up a greater northern Canada.

speechtext:
I would have thought, after
the many times this bill has been before the

House, the promoters would have withdrawn it for good. They must, however, be admired for their persistence. The many times this bill has been before the House I have tried to get some information as to the promoters and as to the need for such a railway. It is a project that does not appeal to most of us and it cannot but be detrimental to the National Railways. As yet we have had very little information forthcoming. Trying to get some information regarding the feasibility of this road, I find that Mr. Lloyd Moore, financial editor of the Toronto Globe, has lately given a detailed account which goes to show that not only is the railway not needed but the whole thing is simply a gigantic swindle.
His article in the Globe reads:
After four days cxf travelling around Red lake, it seems quite apparent that the snow-stakers are showing little interest in real work now that the fictitious market for claims has settled to a more reasonable level. Dome and McIntyre are carrying most of the load. 'Much credit is due Dunlop, Red Lake, for the aggressive policy that is being pursued. Some encouragement has been given in the work done already, and there is a reasonable probability that the outlook will improve as the exploration programme is advanced further. The effort being made by the Dunlop syndicate deserves a more detailed description which will be given out later.
But as to the other great syndicates and those who are responsible for the rush, he says that they are simply marking time. The date of this paper is June 25. The writer goes on to say:
With hardly a single exception, the other syndicates are resting on their oars making no real attempt to fulfil the glittering promises made when Red lake syndicate flotations were in vogue. Here and there small parties are at work, but the whole situation is much 'less active than might be expected, taking into account the obvious importance of the Howey discovery and the favourable geological conditions that prevail over a large part of the Red lake district. The prospectors have not made the most of their opportunity. No work whatever has been done on the many scores of locations that want attention. Some snow-staked ground was sold early in the season at fancy prices and the unsold claims have been left alone. Such neglect does not affect the public as directly as the inativity of syndicates in which investors have placed then-money.
The whole thing seems to be almost a great swindle. As many went in there before the winter was over, much hardship ensued as a result of the fa'se news spread throughout the country by syndicates and prospectors who had no other interest in the whole matter than that of prospectors' earnings. But now apart from all this there is another feature that ought to appeal to this parliament at this time. While we were trying to get some policy laid down by parliament, the former Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) said that

Red Lake Railway Company
they had no interest in the matter. I am sure that the present Acting Minister of Railways, (Sir Henry Drayton), who has taken over his office to-day, after his very exhaustive report of some years ago when he advised that there should be only two railway systems in Canada, will have something to say on this matter. But there is an interesting side for the people of Canada to consider regarding granting charters of this kind.
According to the Canada Year Book our railway debt to-day amounts to more than $2,000 000,000. Many are favouring private enterprise. I think we should encourage private enterprise all we can; but in answer to the hon. member for South Timiskaming (Mr. Armstrong), I want to say that the railways are public utilities and should never be allowed to drift into private hands. The people should keep them under their ownership and control. It has become a habit with some of our big men, bank managers, railway magnates and others, to denounce government ownership, and to denounce the National railways in particular. They would at this time give the National Railways back into private hands because they say it is too costly for the people. The cost to the people will be the same whether it is for private gain or even to make lip a deficit. The substance of these remarks generally is to the effect that the National Railways are too heavy a load for the people to carry, but the fact remains that while our National Railways to-day are showing a deficit annually, the privately-owned system is returning very handsome profits each year. Some 10 per cent dividend is paid year after year by that system and in addition to this very large surpluses are added to reserve. There is no doubt that had both systems been under one efficient management our railways in the year 1925 would have reported a surplus instead of a deficit.
Our railway situation at the present time is something like this. While the taxpayers have to find money to meet a heavy deficit in connection with the national system the earnings from carrying charges as shown by the private concern have left a very handsome profit in the final accounting. The result is that the deficit in connection with the national system and the profits made by the private company are together a heavy burden on the industry of the people, for the extra amount which we have to pay in the form of charges for railway service may be described as taxation. If the railways were all under one management the Canadian people would this year, I repeat, have had the benefit of a surplus in connection with the National Railways.
The dangers attending public ownership seem to be a bugbear to some people. They would take our railways to-day and place them in private hands, but they want to leave the debt for Canadians to bear later on. There is a sum of $2,400,000,000 to-day on which interest must be paid, and it is not likely that any private concern would take over the railways at that capitalization. While speaking on this subject I am reminded of the words of the Acting Minister of Railways (Sir Henry Drayton) contained in the report which he submitted along with Mr. Acworth in the year 1920, to the effect that there should be only two systems of railway in this country from henceforth.
Why should we at this time start another system of branch railways as a result of which we should have probably a repetition of the debacle that now faces us? Facts and figures are sometimes presented in such a way as to mislead the public. The opponents of the National Railways never tell us that the reason for their hostility to the public ownership of public utilities is the fact that it interferes with what they consider the sacred right of some people to exploit the public for private profit. It is certainly strange, as the president of the Canadian National Railways pointed out recently in one of his speeches, that no danger was apprehended when the Canadian National Railways were piling up a huge operating deficits, which their opponents were quite willing to have the country bear. No one appeared to worry over that fact. But now that times have become more stable, now that the country is coming back to normal conditions, there is no doubt that, with the various roads making up the system coordinated and operating as a unified and efficient whole, large operating profits are anticipated. And as the president of the national system remarked, "whispers of death" and other newspaper articles have begun to appear in the press. I quote the words of Sir Henry Thornton:
Can it be that our great financial experts would rather see out national road making tremendous operating losses than see them get out of ^he red ink and operate on the right side of the ledger to the tune of, say, $32,000,000 a year?
According to the Canada Year Book at the end of 1924 the total capitalization of the National Railways has stood at $2,326,411,356 of which $608,624,084 represents stocks, leaving a funded debt of $1,717,787,272. A very large part of this immense sum was lent or given by the government to these roads when they were in private hands and bond issues were guaranteed in respect of it. The part of the debt which is not to-day represented



Red Lake Railway Company
hy earning capacity is as much a part of the puDiic debt as even our war expenditure and should be so considered. The railways should be relieved of this burden. But when we have a project such as this, which is going to add rather than take from the burden of the debt which we now owe on our railways, it is time for this parliament to outline a specific policy regarding our railways. I must confess that I am in favour of government ownership. It has been one of the planks of the farmers' platform for many years and we have seen no reason to change our mind on the subject. When we have such a legacy of debt to meet, bequeathed by the unreasoning optimism of the boom period, which came to an end just about the time the war began, surely we should consider this matter very carefully.
A few years ago it was not safe for anybody to say anything against the boom in railway construction. Anyone who at that time demurred against the credit of the country being granted in aid of railway promoters was thought fit perhaps for a lunatic asylum. Now we have to pay dearly for our ill-considered expenditures during those years. Today the Red lake district is not suffering for lack of a railway. No one knows yet whe1-ther t'he settlement there will be permanent, and as one writer says, those who have gone in there are simply biding their time, leaning on their oars and waiting for somebody else to take the burden of developing the country.
When we were building branch railway lines ahead of settlement our bank presidents did not take the trouble to warn the people of over expansion of our railway system. I must add that they did not refuse to profit by the commissions which were paid them for acting as financial agents for the government or the railway promoters. Nor do the annual statements they now publish show that they have suffered at all by what they call the intolerable burdens the country has to bear. We know the burden of taxation year by year is increased by railway deficits, all because of the indiscriminate granting of railway charters in years past-charters for just such projects as this Red Lake railway. These men boast of their great prosperity, but a glance at the market reports showing the prices at which the shares of their companies are quoted would indicate that they at least are all right while the people are still carrying the burden. The same interests who would transfer our National railways to private control complain bitterly of the additions to our railway debt, but they were absolutely necessary to provide capital to put our railway system into a con-

dition of operating efficiency. There is no doubt that those interests would prefer to see the Canadian National Railways starved so that the country would in sheer desperation be eager to turn the system over as a gift. Those selfish interests would1 be willing to see the Canadian National Railways go from bad to worse until we were willing to abandon the property on any terms. Then our financial benefactors could step in and salvage it on their own terms, but leave the debt on the hands of the public.
Now, when a private corporation finds that as a result of inflation or over-expansion its capital is far in excess of the dividend-earning capacity of the plant it writes the capital down and the shareholders bear the loss. If to-day the capitalization of our National railway system were written down to something like its true value-during the years of the boom we paid at least one-Third too much for all our material-that system would show a profit on operation. A recent noteworthy example of this writing down of capital is the great English company of Vickers Limited, a company of international reputation. Its share capital has been written down some 160,000,000. It would be better perhaps if we put the capitalization of our National railway system at something nearer the real value and earning power of the road. If that system were returned into private hands does any hon. member suppose for a moment that its capitalization would not be written down?

This section 180 is as follows:
Every person who without having a license under this act, then in force,-
(a)	distils or rectifies any spirits, or makes or ferments any beer; or
(b)	assists in disltilling or rectifying any spirits, or in making or fermenting any beer or wash in any unlicensed place; or

This section 180, has been amended by the Statutes 10-11 George V, chapter 52, clause 4 and the minimum fine was then fixed to $200 instead of $100 as it was previously. The government of that day, that is the Department of Inland Revenue, under the direction of a good Tory, absolutely wished to save the hide of his friend, Mr. Plamondon, and as the attorneys had been communicated with as to doubts existing whether the judge should sentence the man to both a fine and imprisonment or simply to a fine, the case was referred to the Department of Justice. Whenever it is provided that the offender shall be liable .to different degrees or binds of punishment, the punishment to be inflicted shall, subject to the limitations contained in the enactment, be in the discretion of the court or tribunal before which the conviction takes place.
The letter to which I have just referred, dated	August 25,	1920,	was signed	by W.Stuart Edwards, Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice. The matter is now in the hands of the Attorney General, and should the latter be willing to permit it, Plamondon will be alb wed to change lids plea so as to enable us to withdraw our charge under section 180.
The other accused parti& have been arrested, and their trial is bound to come up next week. We will keep you informed of any new development.
I respectfully submit, Sir, if ever we have had a gross example of denial of justice, of odious interfering, it is in this case. Here is a man who has pleaded guilty to a charge bearing both a fine and gaol. The judge sentences him to both. Proceedings are started. The accused's attorney, who is no more nor less than the ex-Minister of Inland Revenue himself, the Hon. Mr. Sevigny, who was even Speaker of this House, applies to the same department, to induce them to have the judge's decision changed. As a rule, everybody has a great respect for judges. The courts enjoy the respect of ail, one never interferes, neither directly nor indirectly, nor especially by means of undue influences, in order to shield a political friend. But in this case they want absolutely to whitewash Plamondon and it is requested that the department should bring weight to bear upon the judge. And it is what the department does, by letters, telephones and telegrams, however, without success. It is then that the attorney general shortly after came to a decision, because when a charge is laid before the court, especially when the accused has pleaded guilty, it is not a question of private interests between two parties, but of public right, as for instance, whether the law has been observed or not. Consequently no one had the right to withdraw this charge, no one had a right to prevent the carrying out of the sentence which had been passed by the judge on Plamondon. Nevertheless, for gentlemen who become very scrupulous when they learn that a man has been so unfortunate as to keep three inoffensive little whiskey bottles at home, they are deaf to this state of affairs, they close their eyes and

give us evidence of bad faith by not blushing ten times more than in the case of Moses Aziz!
And still the case goes on. It is real romance this affair of Plamondon. Never did political men take steps with such assurance and with such gross violation of the law, purely and simply to shield Plamondon who was a political friend.
Furthermore, on September 9, 1920, another letter from Messrs. Moraud & Alleyn which is as follows:
Ottawa, September 9, 1920.
Dear Sir,-With further reference to the action taken against Olivier Plamondon, in connection with the seizure o>f stills, we beg to report as follows:
As mentioned in our letter o-f the 3rd of this month, on instructions from you, we applied for withdrawal of the complaint laid against Plamondon, under section 180, and laid a new complaint against hikn, under section 185, on whiiich he pleaded guilty. Mr. Justice Ghoquette then stated that he could not allow us to withdraw our complaint against Plamondon, under section 180, because the latter had pleaded guiilty. He took the case en delibere and rendered judgment yesterday morning. By his judgment he decided that Plamondon could not change his plea of "guilty" to that of "not guilty" on the charge laid under section 180 and that we could not withdraw our complaint. He therefore proceeded to sentence Plamondon to $200 and two months tin jail. The latter has taken an appeal and has been liberated on bail, pending the decision of the court in the appeal. Sentence has been suspended on the charge laid under section 185 until the Court of Appeal has decided the other case.
The Co-urt of Appeal will sit in October. Kindly advise us what your instructions are concerning the appeal entered by the defendant. Will send you a complete report on the Whole matter in a few days.
Yours truly,
Moraud & Alleyn.
What happens next? On September 9, Plamondon was condemned to S200 fine and two months in gaol. What was there to be done to have the sentence commuted? All the witnesses which had given evidence, all the attempts made to try and prevent him from going to gaol having failed, there remained blit one last procedure, a last straw to save the drowning man: it was quickly seized. The Prime Minister of the present government, the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen, stated the other day that the moment a sentence is passed, no one has a right to intervene; well, what happens in the present case?
Steps were taken in order to have the sentence commuted, and they succeeded, for on October 7, 1920, a letter from the Acting Deputy Minister of State is sent to the Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue and later communicated to the crown attorney. The letter is as follows:

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Sylvestre
Canada, Department op Secretary of State,
Ottawa, October 7, 1920. Sir,-Referring to your letter No. 4852 of the 18th ultimo to the Remissions Branch, Department of Justice, dealing wi'tih an aipplioaitdorL of demeney made by Sevigny & Sirois, Barristers, of Quebec-
This is always Mr. Sevigny, the ex-Minister of Inland Revenue and ex-Speaker of the House.
I continue to read the letter:
-cm behalf ocf one Olivier Plamondon, who was racenrtly sentenced by His Honour Judge Choquette to pay a fine of $200 and to serve two months' imprisonment for possessing an illicit still, I am commanded to inform you tihait. his Excellency the Governor General has been pleased to order that Plamondoai be not called upon to serve the sentence of two months' imprisonment, and that he be released from further liability for this sentence as soon as itlie $200 fine has been paid.
His Excellency's decision has this day been communicated to the Solicitor for Plamondon.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
P. Pelletier,
Aching Under-Secretary of State. To the Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue,
Ottawa, Out., Canada.
Here is a man who is sentenced by the jourt- to a fine of $200 and to two months in gaol. An appeal is made, why? The case which I have just submitted is not based on supposition, but on evidence, on facts proven at the Committee of Inquiry on the administration of the Customs Department. An appeal is made but only for the form, for there is evidence to show that little attention was given to this appeal from the moment the sentence of gaol was commuted by the Governor General. The principal reason why Plamondon escaped being lodged in gaol was also established. It is that he, the most guilty one besides being caught in the act, promised, in order to save his hide, to become a Crown witness so as to have four men, who had assisted him, sentenced. He denounced his employees-as it came out in the evidence that these men were employed by Plamondon 

and as a reward for his treachery, his gaol sentence was remitted and he only had to pay the fine of $200. Furthermore: he was given the share which was owed to him as an. informer. He paid the fine to which he was sentenced from the money he received as an informer and he pocketed the balance.
To sum up the case, here is a man who in August is found in possession of three copper stills and another galvanized tin still of a 30 gallon capacity, three lead worms, about 2,000 gallons of wash, 45 gallons of spirits-a sufficient quantity to quench the thirst of many people. This man escapes the severe penalty which he deserved from all angles
and in all justice for the simple reason that he was a political friend of the government, of that day-

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Clause 4 of the report of the special committee is as follows:
Notwithstanding the time devoted by the committee to the taking of evidence the matters referred to it by the order of reference could not be completely reviewed. Much evidence was taken in connection with the port of Montreal; the situation at Beebe and Rock Island, Quebec; and the operation of distilleries. The committee have also with some detail examined Into liquor smuggling in the Maritime provinces. The committee have examined in a general way the conduct of business at certain customs ports of Ontario. The com-

mittee have not dealt, except incidentally, with the middle west and the Pacific coast. To a degree, therefore, this report is incomplete and suggestive rather than final. Full audit and extra-departmental investigation would be profitable in improving the service and recovering a large amount of revenue.
I submit, Sir, that so far as the public of this country is concerned that representation discloses a very distinct limitation in matters as they stand at present. It discloses that the investigation was incomplete in many particulars; incomplete as to the localities investigated and incomplete as to industries investigated, in particular, several distilleries and the business they are carrying on. It is incomplete, moreover, as to the parties investigated; incomplete in fact for the most part with respect to many phases of the subject matter the committee was called upon to inquire into. The evidence was sufficient to disclose that there is great need for a very full, complete and exhaustive inquiry into the evil of smuggling and into the problem of collecting the revenue as it has developed. The people demand to-day that the matter be not allowed to stand where it is at present but that the fullest possible investigation be made from the Atlantic to the Pacific, in order that something comprehensive and constructive may come from the discussion which has taken place in this House. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it would be nothing short of a public scandal if, after the amount of time devoted to this inquiiy by the committee and after the discussion which has taken place in this House with respect to the committee's report, matters were permitted to drop before the public was perfectly satisfied that the investigation had been thorough and complete on all essential points.
May I now draw the attention of the House to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, the minister without portfolio, who at present is administering the Department of Customs (Mr. Stevens). That amendment contains no suggestion of a continuation of the investigation; the amendment is largely confined to a vote of censure on ministers of the crown and is a political amendment purely and simply, evading altogether the matter of primary interest and concern to the people of Canada, namely, whether or not means can be discovered effectively to combat the smuggling evil, to what extent frauds may be taking place in different parts of Canada, and to what extent there is need for redress. I cannot dwell too strongly, Mr. Speaker, on that phase of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, because it illustrates two things: one, that he who has taken

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Mackenzie King
the most interest in the work of the committee evidently felt satisfied when he had completed the investigation at Montreal and the investigating of a few officials from the province of Quebec and one or two officials of the Department of Customs here, but he was not ready to move in this House that an investigation should be continued into the customs ports of such large centres as Toronto and Winnipeg, his own city of Vancouver, and the cities of Halifax and St. John; also was not prepared to advise the House that a complete examination should be made into the affairs of the distilleries that have not been investigated.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that what the public wants is a very full investigation into all the phases of this matter which I have indicated. It was not until the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) moved an amendment that the House had before it the constructive proposal of a judicial investigation to continue the investigation which the special committe commenced-a judicial investigation that would take up the work that had not been reviewed by the committee, and that would also afford opportunity where there was reflection upon the personal character of any man, for him to have a judicial hearing before being condemned in the eyes of the public. That, Mr. Speaker, is an all important feature of the amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; he did have regard for what in British fair play and justice is regarded as all important, namely, that a man whether he be a humble citizen of the land or a minister of the crown, before he is condemned should be entitled to an investigation conducted in a judicial manner and in a judicial atmosphere.
When we on this side were in office we accepted the proposal of a judicial investigation. We intimated that if it were given to us to carry on, that investigation would be made comprehensive, that it would extend to the different centres that I have mentioned and to the different industries to which I have referred, and that it would be made a thorough inquiry, so that this House when it assembled at the next session would have before it the evidence which was taken by that commission, and would also have before it the report of the commission itself, the findings of the commissioners and any recommendations they might have to make, and that the House might be in a position to do something really constructive by way of such further reform as might be considered necessary. However, the amendment was voted down, as the House will recall, by a majority I think of two.
Then what to all intents and purposes was the same amendment was moved by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Fansher), and that subamendment was agreed to and was added to the amendment. May I point out this circumstance to hon. members of the House? When that amendment was carried in that form, the one criticism that I heard coming from the official opposition, and which I heard made also by members of the Progressive group and others in this House, was that that judicial investigation would be carried on by the government of the day, and that the government of the day would appoint as investigators judges in whom they might have confidence, but in whom perchance members of the opposition, members of the Progressive party and citizens of the country generally would not have equal confidence; in other words, that the judicial commission would be a commission chosen by the government of the day to conduct the investigation in a manner that would please the government of the day. That was the criticism that was directed against the amendment as amended as it stood at the time the late administration went out of office. Before going out of office we considered very carefully that phase of the question. We believed that the people of this country would expect the government that undertook the work of cleaning up this smuggling evil to appoint a commission in which there would be absolute confidence, a commission with respect to the findings of which not an hon. member of this House, nor a single citizen of this country, could take any exception. We conferred among ourselves as to the manner in which that all important end could best be attained, and we came to the conclusion that the manner in which that end could best be attained would be through the appointment of a commission of judges, three in number, one to be named by the Prime Minister of the day, the second to be named by the leader of the opposition, and the third to be named by the leader of the Progressive party. I submit. Mr. Speaker, and I wish to say it as emphatically as I can, that I believe it is a commission of that character, and of that character alone, that the people of this country will be satisfied with on this all important national problem. I venture to say that those whom hon. gentlemen opposite, members of the Conservative party, represent, will expect them to name on the commission a judge in whom the Conservatives of this country will have confidence. I know that so far as the Liberals of this country are concerned, they will expect that an opportunity will be given for the Liberals to name
5134	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Mackenzie King
a judge in whom the Liberals of this country have confidence, and I believe that the same will be found to be true with regard to those whom the Progressive members of this House represent, that their constituents will expect them, if the opportunity is offered, to give favourable consideration to an amendment which will give to their leader the right to name on a commission to investigate this all important matter one in whom they have entire and perfect confidence. I repeat that no other commission will satisfy the public demand at the present time. I submit that all the discussion that has taken place in the last few months before the committee of this House, and the discussion that has taken place in this House of Commons has aroused public feeling with respect to the hideousness of certain features of this national evil and national menace.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen say, " hear, hear." Then I say that if hon. gentlemen are sincere in their "hear, hears ' the one way to bring about reform is to give to this country a commission in which the entire country will have confidence. I submit further, Mr. Speaker, that in view of the manner in which this whole question of vital national importance has become a matter of political controversy and of political strife, nothing will satisfy the people of Canada to-day, with respect to settling this question in a proper way other than a commission that will have on it representatives of the three parties that compose this House of Commons. I want the House to stop and consider, as I ask the country to stop and consider, what better guarantee could be given to the nation that the work will be done thoroughly, that the work will be done honestly, that the work will be done effectively, than that each political party in this House will be put in the position of vying with the other political parties in seeing that there is brought to light in the fullest possible way everything that should be disclosed in connection with the existing situation. The late government was prepared to make that proposal had it continued in office.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: When?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Before the
government went out of office, the amendment which was proposed to-day was shown to several hon. members of this House, and it was indicated very plainly that that was the amendment which was intended to be moved from the then government side as a subamendment to the amendment as soon

as opportunity was presented therefor. Such was the case. The amendment which the opposition, through one of its members, has offered to the House today was in the same language and the same words as the amendment which the late government had intended to offer. I say it is due to the people of this country, it is due to these who are represented by the different political parties, that such a degree of confidence as to the thoroughness and fulness of the investigation shall be given to them now that the opportunity has presented.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Do we not consider our judges trustworthy, and is the right hon. gentleman suggesting that each party should name one judge who would be practically a representative of that party?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Assumedly all the judges of the country are trustworthy, but I do say that human nature being what it is, the public would have more confidence in a tribunal constituted in the manner I have suggested, nominated by representatives of all sides of the House than they would have in judges appointed by hon. gentlemen opposite.
May I further direct the attention of the House to this fact: Hon. gentlemen opposite who have been most active in the work before the committee have carried the work just as far as it would suit themselves. If the subamendment to the amendment is not carried we will have to consider the amendment as amended, and that amendment will give to hon. gentlemen opposite solely, and only to them, the nomination of the judicial commission that is to carry on the inquiry. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the public will not have the same degree of confidence in a commission appointed by hon. gentlemen opposite in that way as they would have in a commission appointed in the manner I have indicated. I say that without any desire to reflect on hon. gentlemen opposite because when I had the honour of filling, the position of Prime Minister, in seeking to suggest a commission that would invite and secure public confidence, I proposed to give to the leader of the opposition and to t-he leader of the Progressive party that very opportunity for the reasons I have mentioned.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Did you do that when you
appointed a commission on Maritime rights?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
We will take
one commission at a time. My hon. friends

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Mackenzie King
opposite will have an opportunity to have such a commission if they have not faith in the Maritime rights commission as now constituted. But what I wish to make clear at the moment is that I do believe that nothing short of an inquiry by a tribunal as representative as I have mentioned, conducting an investigation in a manner as thorough as we have proposed, will be satisfactory to the people of Canada.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Will the hon.
member tell us the occasion on which he proposed that the judicial commission he now speaks of should be appointed? I am not asking this for the purpose of challenging his statement, but merely because I want accurate information with respect to it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: I have mentioned that already. I have said that before the government went out of office I had shown the amendment to several members in this House, and those members are within the hearing of my voice at the present time. It was not an amendment I presented, because an opportunity had not been afforded for doing that; it was an amendment prepared in advance because of the criticism that the amendment >as moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, and amended by the amendment of the hon. member for Last Mountain, left to the government of the day, and to the government of the day only, the appointment of the judges who were to compose thaff tribunal.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
On what date
was that amendment drawn up?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I cannot say
offhand. However, I am not standing here for the purpose of being cross-examined; I have given my word and I hope my hon. friend will accept it. May I add this further word as to why that subamendment seemed to me all-important? The amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, as I have already indicated, was aimed1 primarily at passing censure on the Prime Minister and members of the government, at passing censure on the Hon. Mr. Boivin, at passing censure on persons who had no opportunity whatever of appearing to answer charges that might be brought against them. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite when was I, as Prime Minister, told that there were to be charges in the form of censure against myself and members of the administration in any amendment to the report which the House would be asked to adopt? When was the Hon. Mr. Boivin told there was going to be a finding in the nature
of a vote of censure by this parliament? No chance whatever was afforded him to appear before a judicial tribunal and disclose whether or not those charges were well-founded. I stated the other day, and I repeat to-night, that the former Minister of Customs and Excise, Mr. Bureau, states that he is prepared to go before any judicial tribunal.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Why did he not go
before?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
There was not a judicial tribunal of this character for him to go before. However, he asked that I should state on his behalf in this House that he was prepared to go before any properly constituted judicial tribunal and answer for his administration as Minister of Customs and Excise with respect to the particular matters mentioned in the report, and any other matter which could be alleged against him. 1 made the further statement that I thought a commission of that kind1 should be appointed that I thought the Hon. Mr. Bureau should go before such a commission; that he should be heard; that that commission should examine thoroughly into his whole management of the department, and that if the commission found that in any way he was wanting in the discharge of his duties or was guilty of conduct which was not befitting a minister of the crown, I as the leader of the Liberal party would ask him to resign his seat in the Senate of this country and would expect him to do so. I wish to repeat that announcement at this moment. If that commission is appointed on which the Conservative party will have the naming of a member, on which the Progressive party will have the naming of a member and on which the Liberal party will have the naming of a member, I will expect Mr. Bureau to appear before that commission to be examined by each one of those judges, and I will expect this House to have before it at the next session of parliament the finding of those judges upon the conduct, behaviour and administrative character of the work of the late Minister of Customs. If as a result of that finding there should be anything that reflects upon Mr. Bureau's character or upon his management of the affairs of the Department of Customs, then, as I say, I will as leader of . the Liberal party ask and expect him to resign from the 'Senate of Canada. In accordance with the principles of British justice can anything be fairer than that?
As the amendment is brought in this afternoon it applies solely to the hon, member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin) who until two or three days ago was filling the position of
5136	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Mackenzie King
Minister of Customs in this House. The amendment moved by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) does not confine investigation to one minister of customs; it extends the investigation to an examination into the administrations of any or all ministers of customs. It takes the very charges that are being made by hon. members opposite against the hon. member for Shefford and it states to all intents and purposes that inasmuch as the late Minister of Customs has never had an opportunity pi appearing to be heard before a judicial tribunal in his defence in a manner which would' enable him to have his position stated as a judicial body would state it-	_

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: And never been censured by the existing committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
-and as my hon. friend says, never been censured by the existing committee, he should be given such an opportunity before he is condemned in this House. Inasmuch as the committee which brought in this report did
10 p.m. not find that it was possible for a majority of their number to agree upon a censure of the late Minister of Customs, why should this House, without an opportunity of reading the evidence, which opportunity I venture to say none of us has had, without an opportunity of having the benefit of the knowledge which they had, purely and simply for political reasons condemn the hon. member for Shefford in this manner? The public who have a sense of fair play and justice will demand that that course be pursued; they will not be satisfied with any other course than a judicial inquiry. There will always be a lurking suspicion that the amendment of my hon. friend, should it carry, was an amendment moved for purely political reasons. No man or woman in the country will feel secure in his or her mind that real justice has been done to those whose names are mentioned in the amendment.
Further, with respect to anyone whose name is mentioned in the report or in the evidence, I do hot care who he is, be he a member of parliament, be he an official of the Department of Customs, be he a citizen of the country who is neither an official of the government nor a member of parliament, J in any particular there be reflection upon his name or character in what has come before that committee, he too should be made subject to investigation by this judicial tribunal. Can anything be fairer than that? That opportunity should be given to anyone who is named in any way.

I understand that in the committee itself the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy)-and I mention him specially at the moment because I think he will wish to see justice done in this matter-was unwilling to vote especial censure against the hon. member for Shefford, the late Minister of Customs. I ask whether the hon. member for Peace River, having regard to his desire to see justice and fair play done to a fellow member of this parliament, is not going to be satisfied that all the public interest as well as the ends of justice and truth will be rightly served if he along with his leader has an opportunity of naming one of the judges on this commission and the commission is composed also of a judge appointed by hon. gentlemen opposite as well as a judge appointed by the present opposition. These are considerations of a practical and immediate character and should be taken into account at the present time.
More than that, over and over again we have heard, during the course of this late inquiry, query after query as to why it was that only ministers of the late government should have their administration investigated and that there should be no inquiry into the administration of the Customs department when hon. gentlemen opposite had some of their friends and their number at the head of affairs. I do not reflect and I do not wish to reflect upon any previous ministers of the crown; but knowing the character of the men who have surrounded me of late, I do*not propose to say that hon. gentlemen opposite have men of any finer character in their party. I venture to say that an investigation of the Customs department as it has been conducted during the last ten, fifteen years, will bring to light a good many things that will help to explain the situation that we are trying to account for at the present time.
Hon. gentlemen speak about degeneracy in the service. Degeneracy does not start in one or two years; it is a matter of years, and you discover degeneracy only after the evil has had several years to run. The source of degeneracy lies in the past, not in the present. Degeneracy is the fruit of past evils, and I think it will pay this country to have an investigation made that will go back into the past and see how the Customs department was administered under hon. gentlemen opposite. But do you suppose if it is left to my hon. friend opposite to make an inquiry, should by any chance this phantom administration continue, they are going to extend it back into the past? I would have to have more confidence in them than I have at the

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Stevens
moment to believe anything of the sort. So I say, whether we have regard to the subject matters to be investigated, whether we have regard to the extent of the investigation, whether we have regard to the individuals whose conduct should be inquired into, whether we have regard to public officials, ministers of the crown, past or present, the course which has been suggested in the amendment now before the House is the right and proper .course and the only one which will completely satisfy the citizens of this country.
Let me in conclusion say this: If we have to wait till hon. gentlemen opposite get their government into working order we may find in the Customs service new developments which will not be wholly creditable to the country. Ministerial responsibility surely stands for something. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre talks about ministerial responsibility in his amendment. I should like to know what ministerial responsibility we have in Canada to-day. We have opposite four or five hon. gentlemen without portfolios, each one of whom assumes ministerial responsibility for half a dozen departments. I say, Mr. Speaker, it will be a miracle if within the departments of the public service conducted under such management there do not develop difficulties and problems of a character one would hesitate to suggest. I say that the interests of the country demands, not that the invesigation should be postponed until doomsday, but that immediately there should be appointed such a tribunal as I have indicated, which will be able to conduct the inquiry in a thorough, efficient and perfectly impartial manner, and submit to this House such material as may be necessary as a basis upon which to make needed improvements in the public service and to remedy the evils that have been complained of. What is required is a tribunal which will serve the national welfare in a way the country has reason to expect.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Acting Minister of Customs and Excise):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Customs and Excise; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Minister of Trade and Commerce; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
With the concluding
words of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) I am in hearty accord, namely, that a judicial inquiry should be made without delay and should be carried forward to a conclusion with all expedition possible under the circumstances. May I at once direct the attention of the House to the fact that in the amendment adopted unanimously the other evening on the motion of the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Fansher), amending the motion which I myself had made, this recommendation is proposed:
Your commiittee recommends the appointment of a judicial commission with full powers to continue and complete investigating the administration of the Department of Oustoms and Excise and to prosecute all offenders.
The other day my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen), on behalf of his followers in the Conservative party, accepted that amendment in toto, and I am authorized to state to the House now that the right hon. gentleman, as well as this government, will stand or fall by it. This amendment was accepted as a full expression of the wish of those who desire that such an investigation should be in the nature of a judicial inquiry, and it was frankly and freely received and given the unanimous endorsation of the House. Now the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) comes forward and moves another amendment. The hon. gentleman always speaks with great courtesy and skill as well as with moderation, but I would point out that in substance his amendment has for its object not the appointment of a judicial inquiry, but rather the striking out of that portion of the original amendment proposing the censure of those responsible for the breakdown in the Department of Customs in the past. That is the object of the hon. gentleman's amendment; of that there can be no question; and the addition of the words suggesting that the inquiry shall be conducted by three judges is really immaterial.
Let me examine the situation as briefly as possible. What is a judicial inquiry? Under all known' precedents in this country and in accordance with the method which has been followed from time immemorial, a judicial inquiry is one conducted by a member of the judiciary, and it has been universally recognized in the past that the judiciary of Canada were of such a trustworthy character that any judge appointed to inquire into any subject might be expected to make a report that would be genuine and that would meet with public approval. The proposal of the ex-Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is that three judges shall be appointed, of whom one shall have the peculiar confidence of the Liberals of Canada, one the confidence in particular of the Conservatives, and the third the confidence of the Progressive party. I submit that the very nature of such a commission indicates that it will represent partisan or political views. There is no escape from that inference. In other words, the suggestion is that in the appointment of such a commission we shall free these judges of nonpartisan restraint and ask them instead to represent us respectively as Liberals, Conservatives and Progressives.

That has been on the lips of several; my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Dunning) says, " hear, hear." Let me just say a few words in regard to that, and let us look at it very frankly. For four and a half years the late government had absolute, untrammelled access to all the records of that department. For at least two years, or at least eighteen months, they were aware that something was seriously wrong within the department. With that knowledge, with full access to the files, with all the records before them, I ask whether it is fair for the right hon. gentleman to come to the House now and say this committee has not discharged its duty, that it should have dug into the past. If there was anything wrong it was the duty of the late government to expose it. Not only is that the case, but when I made my motion in February the original draft suggested that a committee of the House be appointed to investigate conditions in the Customs and Excise Department within a certain limited time. So far as I was concerned that limit was prompted because of the knowledge that conditions within the department, as the report stated, had been accelerated in the last few years, or had been more pronounced in the last few years. Then the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin), then Minister of Customs, suggested an enlargement of that motion. My right hon. leader accepted that suggestion and no limit was placed beyond which the inquiry should not
rMr. Stevens.]
go. Now I ask the House in fairness to myself whether I should be blamed personally for a delinquency in that regard; I ask the House if it is reasonable to ask me to have done a great deal more than I did-and I am speaking now in the personal vein. I had a certain definite task to perform; I did my best, and while my actions may have been faulty and many others could have done better, I say with a clear conscience that I did my best in the circumstances. Hon. gentlemen opposite placed four men on that committee, four of their own members. Other than sitting in the committee, where only a portion of the work was done, they did not join with me. Most of my work was done outside of the committee, preparing for the work therein. But those members sat on the committee and served well and faithfully; they had every opportunity I had; they certainly had a willing minister to help them; they had everything the minister could give them in the way of files and information, and while I do not say there is any blame, if there should be such I submit to the House that it should not be placed upon my shoulders, but should rest upon their own party.
I think my right hon. friend was not only a little but very unfair to me in the suggestion-I was going to say innuendo-which he made. He said, "Why, the hon. gentleman only investigated one or two ports; he centred his attention on Quebec." I pause at that point to say that there was no suggestion whatsoever of centering upon Quebec. In Quebec we have a city of which I think every Canadian is proud. I am not saying this in specious flattery, but because in Montreal we have a metropolitan city of which any country might well be proud, not only 'because of the beauty of its position but also because of the immensity of its commerce. In that great metropolis there was necessarily a concentration of activity in regard to this matter. You would not go to some little outport to look for the seat of the trouble; it was because this activity converged on Montreal .more than on any other centre in Canada that the investigation was centred there. And 'let me say also that I did my utmost, without support, to uncover the conditions which obtained at Windsor and at Niagara Falls. I did achieve some success, but not very much. I want to say to my right hon. friend, however-and I will deal, with some of these matters in a moment; I do not wish to be too long, but I think it is important more or less to cover the subject-that nearly all of the investigation having to do with liquor smuggling was

centred in the province of Ontario. It is true that the head office of one concern affected was in the city of Montreal, but -the main activities were either on the Atlantic coast o-r along the Great Lakes. So, Mr. Speaker, it is not correct -to say that the investigation centred -only in Quebec.

the House almost isolated, how could he be expected to share in the partisan views of either the Conservatives or the Liberals? That was, I think, very largely his argument. Now I put this in fairness to my hon. friend. Suppose the situation were to be reversed; suppose he were sitting in this House, by the changes in political fortunes, at the head of 100, 110 or 120 members of the Labour party of Canada. Does he not think that in any move that he might make as an individual he would in that case be open to precisely the same charge of being partisan if he proposed or opposed a certain thing? How could he escape that charge? He has a logical and a philosophic mind, and I ask him how, under such circumstances, he could escape that charge. I say this to my hon. friend, and to my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) also, because he made some remarks along the same line:	The only way in which it
is possible for an individual to escape being charged with partisanship is to separate himself entirely from others, and to stand alone as an individual and as a pure independent.

But not very much, either in the nature of progress or reform, in the suppressing of evil in public life, has been accomplished or can be accomplished by individual effort. There must be co-ordination of effort, there must be co-operation amongst those holding common ideas. I ask my hon. friend at least to give me credit for this, that whatever may be the circumstances in which I raised this question, I was actuated by a genuine desire, as I think he has been and is, to do what I could, as I saw it, in what I believed to be the best interests of my country.
Strange to say, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) on the same evening, if I remember rightly, denounced us because we have allowed the estimates of the Customs department to pass last year, and the year before, I think he said. Jacques Bureau when he came into this House with the estimates he was in such a state of health that all of us knew he was not fit to be in the House attending to his duties. My hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton), who was then financial critic for the opposition, came to those of us on the other side of the House at that time and said: "The Minister of Customs is in bad health, and his estimates, so far as
rMr. Stevens.]
we know, are all right." At that time we had no idea whatsoever that there was anything wrong within the department, and the hon. member for West York asked us, as his colleagues, to let the estimates of the Minister of Customs go through with little or no criticism, and that, as a matter of fact, is what happened. There are hon. gentlemen opposite who are gentlemen enough and who are fair enough to agree that these words are absolutely correct. Now my hon. friend from Joliette taunted us that that had been done, that we had let those estimates pass, and he said that because we had allowed them to pass, because we had not criticized the department, we were to blame for the degeneracy in the department. That is not a fair argument. So far as I am concerned I had not the remotest idea, Mr. Speaker, until last winter that there was anything seriously wrong in the Customs department. This grade No. 1-F special to which I have referred is authorized for use in the manufacture of rubbing alcohol compound exclusive^. Let me pause to make this point clear.
