Hon. members opposite say that he was wrong in appealing to the ex-Minister of Customs, and they condemn him in language which I will not repeat. They condemn the hon. member (Mr. Robichaud) out of hand and describe his conduct as inexcusable. Well, if the hon. gentleman has done wrong is not the minister who granted his request still more guilty? That is the whole thing in a nutshell. For the space of a week now, Mr. Speaker, you have been listening to hon. members referring to the ex-Minister of Customs by name, in absolute contravention of the rules. You will at least, Mr. Speaker, acknowledge that in my language in parliament I observe the rules, or 'try to, and that I have always referred to the ex-minister as "the hon. member for Shefford." But right along- and I break the rule now to draw attention to it -it has been said, "Are you going to drive George Boivin out of public life?" This appeal has been made to the House in contravention of the rules and amenities of parliament, and I submit the practice should not have been continued, because after all it is not the person we are attacking, it is not my hon. friend, whose friendship I would cherish, that I am attacking; but I cannot separate him from his office, as I cannot separate my right hon. friend from the responsibilities of first minister which he held for four and a half years, and if we call in question at all the administration's dereliction of duty, then those who happen to be in that position must, forsooth, share that responsibility. Therefore I wish that the House would in considering this question keep away from the personal feature of it and view it wholly in the light of their duty.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth)-I see he is again in his seat-made an eloquent appeal, in the course of which he quoted Edmund Burke's opinion that we should have towards our fellow-beings that feeling of humanity and consideration which recognizes that we are all weak and liable to err, and that there is much good in all men. Now I ask my hon. friend' and other hon. members to listen to these words of Edmund Burke, which I think are far more applicable to the immediate situation before the House than those quoted by my hon. friend, grand and noble as they were. I am reading from the works of Edmund Burke an excerpt from his impeachment of Warren Hastings. Burke said:
There are persona who flattered themselves that the corruptions of India would escape amidst the dissensions of parliament.

Yes, Sir, there are those who would say mat amidst the dissensions of parliament, amidst appeals against persecution, those who have been derelict and recreant in their duty may escape. Then he continues:
What the greatest inquest of the nation has begun its highest tribunal will aoconm>lish.
I call the attention of hon. members to these noble words:
My llordfi, the business of this day is not the 'business of this man, it is not solely whether the (prisoner at the bar be found innocent or guilty, but whether millions of mankind shall be made miserable or happy.
Again I pause. The business of the day, Mr, Speaker, is not the welfare of any individual. The business of the day is this: Shall the fair name of Canada be sullied by those who have been recreant in their duty, and they go not reproached? Shall they? That is the question. Shall the rights of the millions of Canada be passed over simply because w-e do not desire to cast any reflection upon a fellow-member of this House? Burke continues:
Your Lordships will see, in the progress of ithis cause, thait there is not only a long, connected, systematic series of misdemeanours, fount an equally connected system of maxilms and principles invented to justify them. Upon both of these you must judge. According to the judgment that you shall glive upon the past transactions in India, inseparably connected as itihey are with the principles which support them, the whole character of your future government in that distant empire is to be unalterably decided. It wiE take its perpetual tenor, it wiE receive its final impression, from the stamp of this very hour.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, with these words, that just as this House decides in this- matter just so in the future will administrators of departments, those who are appointed to conduct the affairs of this country, be influenced so that in the hour of temptation perchance they will not deal lightly with matters which in this report, which comes out of the turmoil and out of the partisanship- shall I say?-of this investigation, have been demonstrated to' be not in the interests of the country. And so I say to hon. members to-night, let us get away from the idea of personalities. it is most difficult to arrive at an honest conclusion. I want to go back to the country people, to the plain everyday working citizens of Canada, to the people who labour with their hands, to see if I cannot revive within myself some confidence in human nature. Members have come to me almost with tears in their eyes, tremendously excited, telling me that all the evidence was not before us, that there were other and more terrible hidden things which would rise up in the future and haunt us if we took other than

Customs Inquiry

Miss Macphail
one action. I think hon. members have no right to make such suggestions. If there is hidden evidence, bring it out and let us see it. We as members of parliament should' not be asked to pass upon something of which we have no knowledge at all. I do not know whether or not there is hidden evidence; I tried to run many of these rumours to the ground and found a great number of them led nowhere. It may be, however, that they did lead somewhere and I did not follow them to the right place; I do not know. I do know that the things that are being said, the whisperings going on and the members visiting other members in private rooms are not creditable to members of this House or to the institution of parliament.
Although our group may vote in different ways it does not make any difference; we are all trying to get a complete clean-up of this customs affair, and I also want to say that I will not for one moment question the motives of those in our group, with whom I have been associated for five years, who vote differently from myself. I know we are striving for that one thing, a complete cleanup of this customs business.
Now I come to something which pains me exceedingly; I wish I could get out of saying it and I have come to the place where I almost wish I had gone to Europe the other morning; it would have been much more comfortable. I have, however, in agony reached the conclusion that the late government was well aware for quite a period of time-possibly from March to November- that all was not well in the Customs department. It is possible that they knew that Bisaillon was the head of the Montreal underworld and chief preventive officer at one and the same time. I am afraid it is true that it was not until the Stevens motion was mooted that the eleven charges which had been laid against Bisaillon were investigated, and I believe it is true that Mr. Duncan was able to secure the arrest of Mr. Bisaillon four days after he was really given authority to do so. The Department of Customs is the revenuecollecting department of government, doing a business possibly 150 per cent greater than that done by the Canadian National Railways, and one can safely assume that through the corrupt administration of this department large sums of Canadian money were lost. Much as one may feel disturbed about this, or by condemning anyone, it is not a thing that can be lightly passed over or winked at. When we came here at the beginning we entered into a co-operative agreement with the Liberal party, believing it more likely
that we would get the legislation we wanted through that party than through the Conservative party. I happen to be one of the executive of our group, and as such have many times met the executive of the cabinet.
I want to pay a tribute to the actions of those men; they were in every sense of the word kindly gentlemen, and with perhaps one little slip I think were absolutely true to the co-operative pact into which we entered. I want to pay the highest tribute I possibly can pay to those gentlemen for their adherence to that pact, and I want to assure them that more than words can utter I regret the action I am forced to take.
I am not concerned about which party are in power; the fortunes of parties make no difference to me. I do not believe in the party form of government, in fact I do not believe we will ever have good government in Canada until the party system as we know it is broken to pieces. I think if this kind of scrapping and nonsense keeps up that breakup will perhaps be faster than it otherwise would be.
I have a political creed, and it may be of interest to the House to know what it is. I believe we need a change in the form of government which will allow questions to be debated on their merits, and in which the cabinet will be a committee of the House. I believe in good will and the creation of a peace psychology to replace war and militarism. I believe in social credit; I believe that humanitarianism should be expressed in our social laws. I believe in the low tariff. I believe in enabling laws for co-operation. I believe in .electoral reform. I came here to try to work these things out with one party or with the other or with all, and I hope the day is not too far distant when, as sensible human beings, we may be able to vote on the merits of each question and all work together for the good of Canada. At present we have one camp lined up against the other, not working for the good of Canada; I do not think I am going too far when I say that parties do not work for the good of Canada but for the good of party, and I think it time we stopped that nonsense. I believe the people of Canada will also think it time that sort of thing ceased.
I have come to a decision, whether rightly or wrongly, and to that decision I intend to adhere. I am going to vote against the last amendment, and in favour of what is really the Woodsworth amendment plus the Stevens amendment. It is not all I would like; I favour the commission of judges appointed by the three groups in this House, and I think the party now in power might well grant that. I

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Coote
do not think it unfair to say that even judges win their positions through political influence, and if the present government wish to be fair this board should be composed of judges appointed by the different groups in this House.
I have no particular trust in the gentlemen now sitting on the treasury benches; I know that too many of them have also figured in scandals. I would- like to trust them, but common sense tells me that I cannot do so too much. Therefore I think this board should be above criticism by any party, and one in which the people of Canada would have complete trust; I think if the party now in power would accept that suggestion they would go a lonig way towards convincing the people of Canada that they are not trying to make political capital out of this matter but are honestly trying to clean up the Customs department. I do not want particularly to discredit the ministry who vacated their seats yesterday; I do not want to discredit anyone, but I am forced to this action on the very facts of the case revealed in the evidence which I went over in part to-night. So I plead with the present government to go this far; I think they should do so. 1 do not know whether or not they will, but at least I believe they would be doing a good thing for Canada and at the same time a good thing for themselves if they accepted this suggestion.

speechtext:
When this House assembled in January last, Mr. Speaker, neither of the old parties had a clear majority which would enable them to carry on business. They would not co-operate with each other, and if the business were to be carried on it was necessary that the group in this corner of the House should'co-operate with one party or the other. After careful consideration we decided to assist the Liberal government to carry on; we agreed upon a certain programme of legislation, and I think I can claim that I gave consistent support to the government in carrying out that legislation. I may say, however, that had we decided to co-operate with the Conservative party in carrying on the government I would have endeavoured to give them the same measure of support.
When the Customs committee report came before this House, however, we had to deal with an entirely different matter. It was a question of administration, and not a question of legislation. We had not been connected in any way with the administration of affairs in this country. As a matter of fact, the things which are complained of in this customs report happened before we started to

co-operate with the Liberal government. We have to deal with this question on its merits. It has been debated in this House for the past week, and I am not going to debate it to-night for more than a very few mii.utes. I would like, however, with the permission of the House, to review some of the votes which took place on Friday last.
First of all, I could not support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) because it seemed to me that it was avoiding the issue which was placed before us in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), The hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Fansher) asked me to second his amendment. I did so out of courtesy to him and because I approved of the things which were asked for in that amendment. When it was presented to me, Mr. Speaker, I did not consider whether it was in conformity with the rules of this House. It was ruled out of order by Your Honour, and listening to your judgment on that occasion I concluded that you were right in your ruling that the amendment was out of order. Therefore I voted to sustain your ruling, as I have consistently done, I think, throughout this session.
Later on I twice voted for amendments to adjourn the debate. I understand that I have been criticized in some quarters for doing so. After co-operating with that government all through this session, I felt, Mr. Speaker, that I could not do less than extend to them the courtesy of voting for a motion to adjourn the debate if that was desired by that government. Further, Mr. Speaker, you and all the members of this House know very well my objection to this House sitting after midnight; I have made that known on more than one occasion. I hope the time will come when we shall not be compelled to sit to such unearthly hours. On Saturday morning, when the last motion to adjourn the debate was voted on, it was coming daylight. That was not a fit hour for members to decide such a momentous question. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I had reached the limit of my endurance, and I think a great many members of the House were in the same plight. I might add that if this debate were to go on for another week, I think we would all have reached the limit of our physical endurance. For that reason I appeal to all hon. members to try and bring this debate to an end as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, to-day I had the unpleasant duty of being compelled to vote against your

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Marcil
ruling because I felt that your ruling was not right. I do not claim to be very well versed in the rales of the House, but it did seem to me that the rules certainly were not Intended to permit of endless amendments, and possibly because I am so weary of this debate I was opposed to the moving of further amendments. I simply wished, with the permission of the House, to offer this explanation of the different votes which I have recorded in connection with this case up to the present time.
I have listened carefully to the debate on this question for the past week and I have come to the decision regretfully I must admit that the statement contained in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is justified, and I do not see how I can possibly vote against it. I am not opposed to the principle contained in the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), but as its adoption would do away with the amendment which is offered by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, I must oppose it.
May I say, before I sit down, that I hope the members of the late government and the members of the Liberal party will not take it too much to heart. I am voting this way simply because I feel it is my duty to do so, after giving careful consideration to this matter. It is quite possible, Mr. Speaker, that we are not sentencing the Liberal party to any long sojourn in the wilderness. After forty days and forty nights, it is possible they may come back. The people will judge, and we must leave it to the people to decide. So far as I am personally concerned, as I have said before, I am not concerned with the fate of political parties, or particularly with the fate of governments. I am sorry that in this country we have a system of government under which it is impossible for us at times to have a real government, and because of this faulty system we have to-day what somebody has called an imperfect or a makeshift government. But we must do the best we can under this system and until there are enough members come to this House with the determination to reform the system itself, we shall have to put up with it.
We are planed in this difficult position, Mr. Speaker. A very great principle is involved in this case, that is the responsibility of the government to protect the revenues of the country and to give honest administration to every department. It is on that basis, and on that basis alone, that I am casting my vote to-night, if the House will allow us to come to a vote.
Hon. CHARLES MARCIL .(Bonaventure):
I do not wish to give my vote, Mr. Speaker, without a word of explanation. I appreciate thoroughly what has been said by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), and I hope the day will come when our debates will be curtailed and our hours of sitting as well.
I am about completing my twenty-eighth session. I have seen between five and six hundred members of parliament come and go, and parliament renewed seven times, and only half a dozen remain of those of us who were here more than a quarter of a century ago. But the tactics employed then are the tactics that are employed to-day, except that in those days we had two parties, and now we have a third party acting as arbitrator.
As I heard you, Mr. Speaker, give your decision this afternoon it reminded me that ten years ago the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and myself worked hand in hand. There have been occasions in this House during that time, a quarter of a century, when men on great issues rose above party and worked together willingly for the national good, and that was one instance, ten years ago, when the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and those who were associated with him did me the honour of asking me to second a motion that he was submitting to the House for war-time prohibition. It was not popular for a Quebec member to undertake that task. Quebec, consulted in the matter of prohibition, had voted it down by 125,000, but I came here imbued with the idea that during the war time at least, when Canada's efforts were needed to be given to the utmost for the prosecution of the war, prohibition of the importation, manufacture, and sale of liquor, which is at the bottom of all this trouble here since the United States have adopted prohibition, should be enacted. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre and myself did the best we could. He made the best speeches; he always does the best he can, and I backed up my assertions with letters from the whole hierarchy of the province of Quebec, and with thousands of petitions. I thought I had made out a pretty good case, but-strange how things happen in this world -the man who was put up by the govern' ment of the day to move an amendment to the motion moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and myself was the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), who will be Minister of Justice to-morrow in this new government. We took the position that war-time prohibition should be adopted on moral and economic grounds, and showed

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Marcil
the House that our liquor -bill amounted to something over $300,000,000 a year. However, we were voted down, and as I heard you, Mr. Speaker, give your decision this afternoon I was reminded that on that occasion ten years ago the hon. member for West Calgary moved an amendment to the motion moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. The amendment, having been put to the House, carried. After the amendment had been carried I called upon the Speaker, as I find by referring to the Hansard of 1916, to put the main motion as amended. Sir Robert Borden objected, "The amendment is carried," he said, "that puts an end to the matter." But on the following day Mr. Speaker Sevigny gave the decision to which you referred this afternoon, in which he showed that the adoption of an amendment amending a motion is not the end of the story, but that the amended motion must be put, and that is the reason for the debate at the present time. We have never voted on the Stevens amendment, so-called. It has been put by you, Mr. Speaker, to the House for the purpose of enabling the House to amend it still further or adopt it.
I want to say one word about the work of the committee. I think the members of that committee are entitled to the greatest credit. They did the best work that could possibly be expected of them, -but I am sorry to say their work has been incomplete. They do not themselves claim that this investigation is in any way complete. In the early days of the session, following the remarks made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) I called the attention of the Minister of Customs to the fact that in the territorial waters o-f the gulf of the St. Lawrence, smuggling was being carried on -from St. Pierre Miquelon on an extensive scale. These territorial waters are closed waters for the purpose of fishing, but it appears that the extraordinary stand is taken that for smuggling they are international waters, and the result, as we see it, is that schooners drop anchor threee or four miles from shore and keep open bar year in amd year out, demoralizing the population of that district, not only on the Quebec side but on the New Brunswick side as well. That is an important phase cJf smuggling which has not been touched at all by this committee, and one which should be taken up whether this matter is referred to a judicial commission or otherwise.
I do not want to refer any further to the report of the committee because I want to be lenient and merciful to the House. We are

saturated with this discussion on the Department of Customs and1 Excise, and the country is heartily sick of it. The country wants a decision taken and an end put to the whole business as far as this House is concerned, because this question is being dealt with here according to political bias which will carry no conviction to the country; the country will be divided just as this House is divided. To the final decision, rendered by a judical commission of the character proposed, full value and effect will be given.
I am sorry that the subamendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. James is meeting with opposition in this House. I had thought that the wording of the subamendment was so fair and reasonable that it would appeal to the minds of all Canadians irrespective of party. Here is what the subamendment proposes:
The said commission to be composed of three judges, one to be nominated .by the Prime Mdniister of Canada; one by the right hon. the leader of the opposition; and one by the hon. the leader of the Progressive party, said commission to have afll the powers conferred upon such commissioners under the Public Enquiries Act;
The said commission to have .power to make findings and recommendations, and to report the same to parliament at the opening of the next session, .together with the evidence taken 'before said commission.
I think that is a fair proposition, and one that should have met with the approval of all. I have been a long time in the political game, having had forty or fifty years' experience, and I have known judicial commissions appointed by governments in the past that were far from satisfactory to the public at large. In the present instance the commisisoners would be chosen somewhat as the arbitrators are chosen by the parties to arbitration proceedings. I hope the House will accept this solution of the problem and that we will be able then to put an end to the existing difficulty.
I do not want to say any more on this point except to add this: Owing to the adoption of prohibition in the United States the smuggling question 'has become one of the most difficult on this continent to deal with, not only for the Canadian government but for the authorities at Washington. To-day that question is taxing to the limit the efforts of United States prohibition officers, and millions of dollars are 'being spent in the attempt t-o put down smuggling. The adoption of prohibition in the neighbouring republic has resulted in increased smuggling so far as Canada is concerned. I remember when the late Hon. William Paterson was appointed Minister of Customs. In those days the

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bourassa
smuggling was not so extensive as it is today; there was not the same amount of profit in it. If there was no advantage in bringing liquor into the United States, none would be brought; but the higher the tariff was in Canada tihe more incentive there was to smuggling. I am speaking, from experience, and I am well aware that there, are men in this House who know how true it is that smuggling is carried on because smuggling is profitable; when it is not profitable it will to a large extent disappear. That is the reason why the government has been confronted with a problem such as no other government had to deal with in the past.
To an impartial tribunal, freed from the partisan spirit whidh prevails in this House, the case which has been made out by the exMinister of Customs and Excise would carry conviction; it would have that effect with any jury in this country. But the charges have been brought before a political court and if that court renders a verdict it will be political in its nature. I am not unaware of instances of men, held in high esteem by this country, who have been condemned in political courts and yet their honour has not been impaired in the slightest. Nevertheless I hope the House will take this opportunity of constituting a judicial tribunal which will give entire satisfaction to the Canadian public. There is this important fact to be borne in mind as well: the department involved1 here produces revenue to the extent of over $300,000,000 a year, and that revenue must be safeguarded in every respect. I am sure that a judicial tribunal such as I have indicated'could make very important recommendations in addition to those which have been made by the Customs inquiry committee. One of its first recommendations should be to remove from the Minister of Customs and Excise the discretion which the law now gives him. If that discretion had not existed, no such appeals as those complained of would have been made to the late minister or to his predecessors. I myself have knowledge of such appeals, which, indeed, have been made to every member of parliament; and hon. gentlemen supporting for the first time the present government will, if the present cabinet remains in office, find themselves before long, urged to make similar appeals, because there is always a tendency when a man gets into trouble to say, "Give him another chance," and so on. The experience of the past has demonstrated what will haptpen unless the whole system is radically changed, and that can best be done through the findings of a judicial commission.
I am going to vote for the subamendment with the greatest satisfaction, because I know it is in the interest of the country. On the other hand I will vote against the amendment of tihe hon. member for Vancouver Centre because I deem it to be nothing but a political move.

I hope the next time the people of Canada are appealed to, whether it be this summer, this fall, or next year, -they will have something else to deal with than these matters that will no more be properly

exposed to the people than before this House by the work of this committee, good men as they are, or by the debates that take place in this House. I hope that in these few words I have made myself clear to the members of this House and to the people whom I represent.

The case is never given to the jury until the whole evidence has been completed. In this report, which I understand was a unanimous one by the committee, clause 4 states:
No/t withstanding the time devoted by the committee to the taking of evidence the matters refrrd to it by the order of reference could not be completely reviewed.
I ask any man who has a sense of British fair play:	Are we going to condemn a man
or a group of men until the evidence is completed? I am taking the committee at their own words. speechtext:
I do not blame the
hon. member for Mackenzie, because I might have done the same thing myself. Members of parliament are in duty bound to represent their electors, and if an elector who is in trouble seeks advice, it is only right for his representative to put his case before the minister concerned, whose duty it is to listen to such representation. If we do not want ministers of the crown to have any power of discretion in the future, then let us so provide by law and let us inform the public accordingly. Electors expect members of parliament to do anything and everything and I hope my voice will carry throughout this Dominion when I say to-night that if the people expect their representatives to make certain appeals on their behalf they must not turn round and condemn them afterwards.
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for St. James is to my mind the fairest that has been submitted in this debate. It gives to the group in this comer an opportunity to have some say in the appointment of the commission. This is the first time in the history of parliament that it has been proposed that any minority group should participate in such an appointment. Am I going to throw that precedent away? It seems to me a healthy state of affairs that different groups should be consulted in a matter of this kind. This is the conclusion to which I have come after serious reflection. I may be wrong in the eyes of some people but I am acting conscientiously. The ex-Minister of Customs was probably indiscreet, but I refuse to admit for ,a moment that he is open to censure. I have sat with the 'hon. gentleman in this House for the last five years, having come into contact with him both personally and in his official capacity as minister of the Department of Customs, and speaking from my experience of him I believe that the honesty, the integrity and the ability of the hon. gentleman are beyond question. Certainly his ability he has demonstrated in this House; and of his honesty I am convinced from personal experience. I do not think it would be according to British fair play to condemn the minister as proposed in the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. I do not take any stock in the rumours one hears around these corridors. They do not amount to anything in my estimation. Let us have a proper judicial
commission before whom all the facte can be brought out to the satisfaction of the country, and let members of that commission represent impartially the views of the parties constituting this parliament. I did not want to speak at any length to-night but I could not let this occasion pass without putting myself on record and paying the ex-Minister of Customs the tribute to which I think he is entitled.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: I declare the subamendment lost. The question now is on the amendment as amended.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you put the question I desire to say a few words thereon. I am satisfied that every hon. member is exceedingly anxious that the judicial commission which is to be appointed by the acting government shall be of a non-partisan character. There is no doubt that it should be such. I would therefore suggest that the time is not yet too late when the acting government may accept an amendment which will allow them to go to the country feeling that at least their commission will have the confidence of the people. Like the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Maophail), I have very little confidence in either of the political parties as such. I have a great deal of confidence in several hon. members of both parties. I am not willing, nor do I think the public will be, to accept the findings of a royal commission appointed by the Conservative party any more than I would be ready to accept the findings of a royal commission appointed by the Liberal party. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) :
That the amendment as amended be further amended by adding thereto the fallowing words after the words "and to prosecute ail'l offenders":
and fchait such judicial commission should consist of a judge to be named by the two judges of the Exchequer court of Canada, ithe said judge aoting as a commission to have ail the powers conferred ujpon such commission under the Pub Lie Inquiries Act. The said commission to have power to make findings and recommendations and to report the same to parliament at the opening of the nexit session, together with the evidence taken before the said commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I simply rise
to say that this amendment is one which, it seems to me, this House can accept; the government certainly can accept it. Our idea is to have a commission just as impartial as we can get it. We do not want partial judges; we do not want judges named by this or by that party, to fight one with the other. We do want to get a commission as impartial and as far-reaching in its effects as is possible,

Customs Inquiry-Division
and the hon. gentleman 'has found a means of taking away the selection of this commission from politicians of all stripes; on behalf of the government I have much pleasure in accepting it.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: I wish to congratulate the hon. gentleman who has moved this subamendment. We cannot have too many safeguards from the present government, and if the leader of the House had not accepted the amendment I would have supported it on division. When I consider the past records of these gentlemen, royal commissions have been instituted under Tory regimes in the past-and I wish gentlemen sitting to my left to remember- this-reports were brought in, and those found guilty are still sitting in this House supporting my hon. friend.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I do not wish t'o detain
the House on this question, but it is quite apparent from the amendments which have been offered that members of parliament have no confidence in their ability to appoint a commission; neither have the government. I think the only proper course to take in the circumstances would be for this parliament again to appeal to the final arbiters, the electors of Canada, and if this amendment were not before the House I would move that that be done. Since this amendment is now before us, I cannot do so.
Amendment (Mr. Garland) agreed to.

speechtext: Sir HENRY DRAYTON moved the adjournment of the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask my hon, friend one or two questions? Is it the intention of the government that the House shall sit on the 1st of July?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: In connection with the business of the House, Mr. Speaker, it has become now entirely a matter for the House, and we would very much like to have the opinion of the House. So far as I know, we have got rid of the only contentious matter remaining before parliament. I do not think there is anything at all contentious remaining on the order paper. We have the estimates, which are my right hon. friend's estimates, and we are prepared to put them through. In addition to those estimates, we have the legislation of my right hon. friend which is here in this House or in the other House, and we are prepared to do everything we can to facilitate that. In other words, so far as we are concerned I see no reason why this House should not close its business to-morrow night, but that, of course, is entirely for the House to say. If on the other hand parliament thinks there are a lot of other matters to be discussed, that we have not been here long enough, or that there are some contentious issues arising out of my right hon. friend's own estimates or legislation, why then the government is perfectly willing to sit on the holiday if the House desires. But if we are to have a lot of contentious business brought on, perhaps it is not worth while sitting on the holiday.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In connection with the legislation, does my hon. friend include the bill for the transfer of the natural resources to Alberta, which appears on the order paper as a resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
We have not as yet had time to go into what has been done by my hon. friend in that connection, but it has been noted. We do not propose to take any action one way or the other in the dying days of this session in connection with that legislation.
' Mr. MACKENZIE KING: That means no action?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No action this session.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That will be gratifying, I am sure, to our friends from Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, they will not be shocked, because they have been gently prepared by no action at all on the part of gentlemen opposite, who have had lots of time to act, which we have not had.

Private Bills

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend what business is proposed to take up to-morrow, and in what order?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We have some bills that I think should be got rid of. There is the bill in connection with the Montreal harbour commission, and a bill regarding which my hon.' friend the ex-Minister of Finance has been good enough to send over to me to-night a memorandum, having regard to the Civil Service Superannuation Act. Apparently that is a bill about which there should be very little trouble, and I take it from what his memorandum discloses that it is something which should be disposed of. I think we ought to facilitate all the legislation which ought to be handled at all.
You are very nice indeed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
My hon. friend is
a little late in paying me that tribute, which I know the House feels I so wonderfully deserve. After that we shall take up the estimates. We know there will be very little trouble about my right hon. friend's own estimates, but we shall be governed very largely by their criticism.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
May I suggest to the
House while it is in the mood for passing bills and estimates holus-bolus, that perhaps after the six months we have been here this session it is about time the report of the special committee appointed last year to reduce the length of the session and reduce the length of speeches was adopted.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
There is only
one other question my right hon. friend asked that I did not answer. He asked whether we would sit on the holiday. So far as the government is concerned, if the House cannot get closed up by to-morrow night, but wishes to go and wind up the work of the session as quickly as possible by sitting on the holiday we are content to work on the holiday.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 1.15 a.m. (Wednesday).
